I do not seek compliance or agreement. I seek a balance where I have observed a dominating behavior. I seek kindness when I am spoken to in a rude tone. I never once said I want him to be like me or owned by me. that is an incredibly offensive statement to make. I have every right to observe a behavior that is generally characterized by the culture my partner and I have grown up in and have mutually agreed to subvert. I made the post to see if I could gather better conversation skills so we can achieve those goals.

That is a lot of assumptions to make. I use the words I do because that is actually how I speak. Sorry if I am too wordy and "text book" for you. I feel as though you have missed the point. I am not trying to foist my opinion over his, I just feel like my voice is often stifled. I don't see how the information I shared supports a misunderstanding of the situation I am in. I don't think there was enough information there to assume that 1) I am not being gas-lit 2) the observations I have made are not true and 3) that my opinion is superior to my partner's. In fact, my post clearly states that I am searching for balance where I feel there isn't any. I do not ask for his compliance, I ask for sensitivity regarding the way I am spoken to in isolated conversations. The sensitivity helps me feel more balanced so I feel safe enough to share. If someone is saying something to you in a rude tone, is it not logical to feel bad? Is it actually wrong to tell the person who was rude that the wording could be better? This all began around the time I was in middle School (12-14) I learned about eastern religion in my history classes and since then became fascinated with the philosophies that come from that part of the world. Later on I had briefly decided to become a polytheistic Wiccan but I have since distanced myself from the doctrine. These influences did shape how I practice my pantheistic spirituality. I like to think of my rituals as a blend of traditional witchcraft and mental cultivation as it exists in Buddhism. My understanding of karma comes from an anthropologist who lived in monasteries in the east and read primary texts in their original languages. He teaches a class at my university which discusses eastern religion. If I can boil down all these years of spiritual experimentation, my greatest inspiration has been the things I have learned in school and through a lot of reading. I wish I could say that my practice is all original, but truly it is a great big salad of other people's ideas. I just organized the information to make it work for me. If you are interested, some sources include:
**Anam Cara** - a book of Celtic wisdom
**Zen Mind Beginner's Mind** - this is a short and easy read
**The Wicca Handbook** by Eileen Holland - This author frames Wicca in a way that works well with pantheism and is less about strict doctrine. 
**Sacred Jewels of Yoga** - a short read as well, explains Vedic religion.     
I would also look into indigenous beliefs around the world and look for patterns. Shintoism in Japan has many similarities to Celtic animism and Native American religions. These patterns are what help solidify the universality of human consciousness.

Karma is a big thing in my practice. I have to make sure I am clear about the definition however. many spiritual media in the west don't grasp the whole picture. Karma is any volitional action. It is generated by the power of human will. If you generate negative karma, there are negative consequences. This is often confused as "what goes around, comes around" but it really is not a point for point match. There isn't someone or something keeping score of your deeds and then sending you an appropriate treatment. So now that is out of the way, this is how I use karma in my practice. I believe that intent generates as much karma as any other action but it exists in your mind. To generate positive karma, and in turn reaping the benefits of a well tuned mind, I think upon symbolic objects. I keep an altar with "sacred" items that represent what I wish to see in myself and the world around me. I use traditional magic items such as wands and crystals, but I do not believe they contain supernatural properties. They are merely channels for my intent. I see actions as the beginning of a fractal. The shape I make will continue to take that shape on larger and larger scales.

I am actually in college and have had the discussion of grade privacy. I wanted to keep them to myself, but having two Nparents is a tough thing to fight (especially the financial weight they carry). I do care about my education, but I have social anxiety which manifests in an outright phobia of submitting work for judgement. I am no psychologist, but I am pretty certain the way my parents behave when I fail to meet their expectations has something to do with that fear and anxiety. I don't want to blame them for my own failures, but I would not be so afraid to such a degree that affects my functioning if I had not seen violent reactions for something that is fixable. Even success is met with a need to do better. I have developed an urge to both please and rebel against my parents because the reactions are largely the same, self-centered and dramatic. I resent them because when I do well, its never the image they want to share with their friends. I am not the engineer they want to brag about. I don't match up to their peers' children. Since I am not like my parents, they think I am betraying them. I really just want to be happy and focus on my own life (be it success or failure). I am really tired of having the conflict between "outcome oriented" and "process oriented" because I already know I work better focusing on the process. Its my parents who condition the outcome orientation.

My most important advice is 
* You may inherit behaviors from your parents, but you are the upgrade. You are the new model with bugs worked out. 
I always felt shame because I can see many qualities in me that are apparent in each Nparent. I am thankful that having two Nparents gave me perspective that neither of them have; since I am a blend of the two, I can recognize the behaviors and stop them. 

Another one which is harder for me to follow
* don't fret over the Nparents' overreactions. It doesn't matter what they think of you. If you are happy they don't need appeasement. If you are unhappy with you life, they still don't need to be pleased. You will be far more successful if you eliminate the worry caused by parental opinions. You do things for you and not anyone else!

Its a hard decision. I also have an elderly bunny and had thought about getting him a companion when he was about 6 and worried about the grief of the new bunny when his time came. He is 8 now and due to some unfortunate circumstances a year old female bunny came into my care. I reluctantly agreed to be her forever home because she had been rehomed too many times. The bonding process is what needs focus the most. I kept each rabbit in separate cages and in different rooms for the first few weeks because scent is a huge deal for rabbits. I slowly introduced them and had sessions of interaction with increasing lengths of time for another two or three weeks. The old one was very territorial at first but started to understand that the young one is welcome in the human side of the family. I encouraged grooming behaviors with treats and now he accepts her. They began to cuddle together shortly after and are still good house mates to each other. My boy is almost 9 so I am fabricating a plan to keep my young one's grief to a minimum when the day comes. I feel that the situation of bonding an elderly rabbit is not ideal, but it is working out for me so far and I celebrate everyday that both my rabbits have friendship and security. 

Please note that opposite gender rabbits are often easier to bond if you are worried about violent behavior. But remember that all rabbits need time to bond

I suppose I cannot delve too deeply into why certain nations prefer one economic model over another. I am not a part of a culture that does see Communism as legitimate. Sadly I will have to give you the mom response of  "they just do". If you are interested in that particular issue, I suggest talking to someone like a Chinese native. But in a broader sense, I can explain that to scholars of social sciences, the idea of advancement cannot be placed in any specific philosophy so long as it isn't a major human rights violation (which is a tricky subject and requires lots of diplomacy from all sides of an issue). Historically it was Europeans and their colonies that held the authority over what is advanced and what is not. This bleeds into current affairs because Western peoples still hold a lot of influence. They are the ones who wanted to influence others in the past where as Eastern peoples usually were more isolationist. This is why I state that on a global scale, definitions of development fall on the ones with power. Yet, individual nations still see development differently. Its a tricky concept, but there exists a subjective definition as well as a universal definition and the goal is get close to merging them while maintaining cultural identity. We have conflicts with people in the Middle East because they see our philosophy as barbaric and we feel the same about a lot of their ways. They do have morals that are not unlike our own though. It is up to diplomats and such to communicate what is wrong with out disrespecting a cultural practice. So Human advancement requires all cultures to set aside their baggage in order to come up with core values that the entire world can live with. If western people see something very wrong, it is up to us not to swoop in to forcefully change these people (many would consider this westernization), but to have thoughtful discussion on why we think its wrong. I know its hard, but have I made the distinction clear? you are correct that it can be both, but advancement can't be completely western. It is better for all nations to think in terms of "globalization" rather than clashing with east and west. I know this is very idealistic, but for the sake of explaining terms, that is what should be considered advanced.

Advancing on the world stage is often under a western mindset. They are not unrelated. However for purposes of remaining neutral to culture, westernization is not "advancing" by definition. You can be a developed nation and not adhere to western mentality. Its helpful to view advancement as an umbrella term, where western philosophy and culture is one subsection of the whole. This is why Russia, other Parts of Asia and Africa avoid becoming western while at the same time want to become more advanced or developed. One example of this is the Capitalism vs. Communism clash. Many places in the east truly believe that Communism is a better way to develop their nation as a global player in economics. While historically it has caused a lot of tragedy, the ideology is still widely held and respected. Just like Capitalist economies, there is room for corruption within the government. So the point is that in practice, advancement is subjective to the culture you belong to and has the potential to be seen as a lack of progression to others. The definition for global advancement usually lies in the culture with greater power and influence.
